title: The Blaschka Object Network — Harvard Receiving Craft Ecology Register
scope: A source-controlled reconstruction of the local craft, museum, administrative and patronage capacities that converted shipped Blaschka models into stable Harvard museum objects. This register distinguishes an external Cambridge carpenter/builder workshop (John Waugh), museum-based technical continuity (Louis C. Bierweiler), donor handling (Mary Lee Ware), curatorial handling (Goodale/Ames), customs authority and broker coordination.
analytical_guard: 'Receiving craft ecology', 'contracted craft capacity', 'procedural memory' and 'embodied handling memory' are project analytical terms. Do not describe Waugh as Harvard museum staff unless a direct appointment source is found; the 1907 Cambridge directory and Goodale correspondence instead show an independent workshop. Do not call Bierweiler a registrar/conservator in the early period; later titles must not be back-projected.

comparative_structure.field_side: Rudolf's Jamaica travel borrowed Boston Fruit Company's commodity infrastructure; cargo schedules and local company personnel shaped scientific movement.
comparative_structure.receiving_side: Harvard borrowed Waugh's local cabinetmaking/building workshop while developing museum-based Bierweiler expertise; external and internal craft capacities jointly shaped fragile-object handling.
comparative_structure.interpretive_result: Scientific/artisanal mobility attached itself to infrastructures built for other purposes at both ends. The relevant infrastructures were not only carriers and customs systems but also local workshops able to fabricate cases, supports and exhibition furniture.

Ames 1924 explicitly cites long training, mounting technique and Museum traditions
memory_types.failure_mode: not directly observed in a breakdown case; value is visible in reliance and praise

memory_types.evidence: independent workshop, employees, recurring case/plaque/moving/packing contracts
memory_types.failure_mode: 1907 illness temporarily creates a 'heavy handicap' for Goodale's photographic/museum work

research_observations: The receiving end was neither a single institution nor a single profession. It was a mixed ecology of patron hands, curator decisions, customs authority, broker paperwork, an external cabinetmaker's shop and an internal museum assistant.
Waugh and Bierweiler should not be forced into a simple succession. Their evidence instead shows a shifting boundary between contracted craft capacity and museum-based technical continuity.

The 1907 appendicitis episode is a small natural experiment: Waugh's temporary incapacity becomes a 'heavy handicap' because moving models and other practical operations depended on a local craft contractor.

Ames's 1924 description of Bierweiler's 'long training' and familiarity with Museum traditions is unusually direct evidence that museum infrastructure consisted partly of remembered technique embodied in a worker.
The Blaschka transport history therefore connects commercial infrastructure, documentary infrastructure and craft infrastructure. Moving a fragile representation required all three.
